# Vignette: Priya

Priya is a 44-year-old South Asian woman who works the morning shift at a large home goods store in a busy suburban shopping center. She has been married for nineteen years, has two teenage sons, and until three years ago, describes herself as someone who rarely worried about much. She was, by her own account, "the steady one" — the person her husband called when something went wrong, the coworker others gravitated toward during a stressful inventory week. That version of herself feels very far away now.

Three years ago, Priya was working a regular Tuesday afternoon when a man two registers down from her pulled a gun on her colleague, a young woman named Dani who was barely twenty-two. What followed lasted less than four minutes. Priya stood frozen behind her register, close enough to see the trembling in Dani's hands, close enough to hear the sounds she made. The man fired once before fleeing. Dani survived, but only after weeks in the hospital. Priya was uninjured. She has never quite forgiven herself for that fact.

In the days after the shooting, Priya told herself she was fine. She went back to work within the week because staying home felt worse — the silence of the house gave the images nowhere to go. But the store had changed, or she had. The sound of a cart rattling across the floor could send her pulse spiking. A customer reaching into a jacket pocket made her step back without thinking. She began positioning herself near the back stockroom whenever she could, away from the entrance, away from the registers. Her manager noticed she was avoiding the front of the store but said nothing directly.

At home, Priya moves through the evenings in a kind of careful exhaustion. She sits with her family at dinner but finds herself watching the front door. Her husband, Rajan, has learned not to come up behind her unexpectedly. He tries to be patient, but she can see the worry in his face, and that worry becomes its own burden. She has stopped sleeping in their bed most nights, drifting to the couch after midnight when the dreams wake her — not always the shooting itself, but variations: Dani's face, the sound, the moment of helplessness that replays with small and terrible differences.

Priya does not talk about what she saw. Her mother, who calls from Chennai every Sunday, asks why she sounds tired. Priya says it is the early shifts. In her cultural world, she explains carefully, you do not bring this kind of thing into the open — you manage it, you carry it quietly, you do not want to be seen as someone who cannot cope. There is also a layer of shame she struggles to name: she was not the one who was hurt. She tells herself she has no right to be this undone by something that happened to someone else.

And yet she is undone. She has stopped meeting friends for the occasional dinners they used to share. She finds crowds intolerable in a way that embarrasses her. Last Diwali, she left her sister-in-law's gathering early because the noise and the press of people made her feel she couldn't breathe. She told everyone she had a headache.

At work, she is still competent — she knows the job, she shows up, she helps customers find what they need. But a part of her is always scanning, always calculating the distance to the nearest exit, always braced for the moment the ordinary world tears open again the way it did on that Tuesday afternoon. She is tired of being braced. She is tired of the vigilance that never turns off, of loving her family from behind a pane of glass she cannot seem to break through. She wants, more than anything, to feel safe in an ordinary room. She is not sure she remembers how.
